newsitem.title: HONG KONG: UNHCR appeals over Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR appeals over Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) will urge resettlement countries at a Geneva meeting on May 26 to take in Vietnamese refugees remaining in Hong Kong, a local legislator said on Monday.
"The High Commissioner and also the Assistant (High) Commissioner...will...make a special appeal to all the resettlement countries," legislator James To told reporters.

He said the news came from the head of UNHCR's Hong Kong mission who attended a session of the Legislative Council's Security Panel at which lawmakers lobbied representatives of nine countries to take more Vietnamese refugees from the territory.
UNHCR spokesmen in Geneva could not be reached for comment.
But representatives of the nine countries at the Hong Kong session, including the United States, Australia and some European nations, promised no fresh commitment to admitting refugees, To said.

One of them even told the panel the refugees in Hong Kong were given a low resettlement priority given that there were hundreds and thousands others living in worse conditions overseas, he said. To declined to name the country representative.

Legislators in the panel also urged the Hong Kong government to ask Britain, as the current colonial power, to take all the Vietnamese boatpeople and refugees remaining in the territory when it reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
They might reprimand Britain if it did not do so, To said.
Another legislator, Cheung Man-kwong, said: "If Britain doesn't do it, Hong Kong can ask the United Nations to reprimand Britain as being irresponsible."
There are now some 2,700 Vietnamese boatpeople in Hong Kong detention camps. Another 1,300 are being cleared as genuine refugees and are awaiting asylum in third countries.
The U.N. Assistant High Commissioner for Refugees, Sergio Vieira De Mello, said earlier this month that some 1,500 Vietnamese asylum-seekers would remain in Hong Kong after the handover.
Of them, 1,000 were being classified as refugees and the other 500 as illegal immigrants.

Hong Kong, a British colony for 156 years, reverts to China in a little over six weeks time. China has repeatly told Britain and the colonial administration that all Vietnamese detention camps would have to go by the handover.
The main barrier to acceptance of the refugees is that about 900 have criminal records and others have histories of drug addiction, To said.
The government's efforts to clear the detention camps have also been countered by a surge in Vietnamese illegal immigrants, he said.

Sally Wong, Hong Kong government's refugee coordinator, was quoted by television as saying authorities had intercepted 772 illegal Vietnamese immigrants this year. But the news report gave no comparative figures.

The boatpeople are the last of a human floodtide of tens of thousands who have fled their homeland to Southeast Asian territories, many aboard flimsy boats, since the communists won the Vietnam War in 1975.
